transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-16
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE note), Dana Morris (Cascade - Head of ML), Ethan Liu (Cascade - Infra Lead), Priya Shah (Cascade - Finance), Liam O'Connor (Cascade - Data Scientist)

Summary (auto): high-level cost econ discussion, some rough numbers thrown out, agreement to run benchmarks and exchange security docs.

00:00 Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um gonna kick off, quick intros, then jump into cost econ which I know is top priority for you all.
00:12 Dana: Hi all, Dana here. We want to understand if Redwood hosted or dedicated makes sense for our quant models and the chat features, really around unit cost.
00:20 Samir: Great, thanks Dana. Topline — we usually compare three buckets: Hosted (pay as you go), Dedicated (reserved GPUs/pools), Private (VPC or on-prem). Today we'll walk through per-token math and levers like batching and KV/prefix caching.
00:38 Ethan: Quick context from infra — we have a 10k qps spike pattern in market hours, average seq len 512 tokens for internal work, but some queries go to 3k tokens for long context. Budget is constrained, Priya's on call.
00:55 Priya: Yep budget is the limiter. We can do a monthly commit if it reduces unit cost significantly but need clear ROI.
01:10 Avery: Cool. Starting with hosted — typical per-token examples (these are illustrative): for a 3B open model type, hosted text-gen might be around $0.0006 per input token and $0.0009 per output token at baseline; totals vary by model and seq length. Larger models obviously higher.
01:34 Liam: When you say "per-token" is that aggregated input+output or split out?
01:38 Avery: Split out usually, but we show combined cost lines in the spreadsheet. We'll send exact breakouts.
01:45 Samir: On the levers — batching can reduce per-token CPU/GPU overhead. For example with 4-8 request batching at the runtime level, you can see 20-35% drop in token cost for throughput workloads. Prefix/KV caching is enormous for repetitive prompts — if you cache first N tokens on the server, downstream requests only compute incremental tokens which can drop cost by 50-80% for those flows.
02:10 Dana: Our waterfall uses repeated system prompts and a lot of shared context; caching sounds promising. But how does it work cross-tenant and with compliance?
02:20 Samir: Cache is configurable — can be per-customer, route-level. For hosted, we offer route isolation and TTLs, plus control over what gets cached. For Dedicated or Private you get full control on eviction policies and KV encryption.
02:36 Ethan: For Dedicated, what's the ballpark committed spend to get good per-token numbers?
02:40 Avery: Typical starting point is reserved pool equivalent to ~4-8 A100 GPUs or the modern equivalent; pricing depends on region and instance. In our example sheet, committing to a mid-size dedicated pool pushes per-token down 30-50% vs hosted for stable, high-throughput workloads, especially when you use aggressive batching.
02:58 Priya: Can you put some numbers — like if we commit $40k/month what does that look like?
03:05 Avery: Sure at $40k/mo committed, assuming heavy usage patterns and batching/cache, we can model to maybe ~ $0.00025-$0.0004 per token effective, again depends on model family and seq lengths. With hosted at lower volumes the per-token may be higher. We'll show a sensitivity table.
03:29 Dana: Are there additional infra charges for data egress or storage with Private?
03:34 Samir: For Private there can be infra and licensing components — CAPEX for on-prem or VM costs for VPC. We include a KMS integration fee and audit log retention costs sometimes as addons. We'll map them out.
03:48 Ethan: Latency impact? Batching improves cost but will increase tail latency — how do you balance?
03:55 Samir: Right that's the classic tradeoff. We expose batching policies per-route: you can set target latency SLOs and the runtime will try to balance batch size vs wait time. For low-latency routes you can use smaller batch sizes and accept higher cost; for bulk jobs you can batch aggressively.
04:16 Liam: For our 3k token requests, does KV cache help much? There's less prefix repeated.
04:21 Samir: Less, yes. KV helps most when initial prompt or long system context repeats. For long distinct contexts you rely on batching and kernel selection/quantization. Quantized model variants (int8, etc.) also reduce token compute cost.
04:38 Dana: Can you share examples of quantized vs full fp32 cost deltas?
04:44 Avery: Typically quantization can drop GPU memory and improve throughput; cost can drop ~20-40% depending on model and accuracy tolerance. We'll include model/quality tradeoff recommendations.
04:58 Priya: If we start with hosted and then migrate to dedicated, what's the migration friction?
05:04 Samir: We aim for near-seamless migration — same API surface, model pinning, and routing policies. You can start hosted, route steady traffic to dedicated when committed, and Redwood handles routing and KV state compatibility with a short cutover. There are edge cases but we help with runbooks.
05:28 Ethan: We need SSO/SAML and audit logs, we assume that's standard?
05:32 Avery: Yes, Hosted supports SSO, role-based access, and audit logs for enterprise tiers. Dedicated and Private give deeper controls and can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Samir will share the security pack.
05:45 (15:12) Jordan: Quick note, I'm going to drop a short doc link in the chat with cost spreadsheet template and sample runs.
05:53 Dana: Great. Let's go into a quick worked example — we had a sample baseline: 200M tokens per month, average seq 512, mix of gen vs embeddings.
06:05 Priya: Our budget target is to keep unit cost under $0.0005 effective per token including overheads.
06:12 Avery: Ok with 200M tokens, hosted might be around $0.0006-$0.0008 per token, so monthly $120k-$160k. With dedicated and caching that could be brought to $50k-$80k depending on cache hit rates and batching.
06:33 Dana: That's a big delta — what hit-rate do you assume?
06:36 Avery: In that example we model a 30% cache hit. If you get to 60% for many dialog flows you hit much lower effective costs.
06:44 Liam: How accurate are these numbers? Are they from internal benchmarking?
06:47 Samir: Mix of public benchmarks and our internal runtime tests. We can run a short benchmark with your workload to get precise numbers.
07:00 Ethan: For the perf test, what do we need to provide?
07:03 Samir: A representative request trace or sample dataset, access window for a few hours, and a VPC peering if you want private network tests. We'll run tests on a reserved pool and show latency/cost curves.
07:16 Dana: We can share traces but scrubbed. Security ok?
07:19 Samir: That's fine, we have NDA in place and we can sign any additional agreements.
07:24 Priya: On accounting — how are tokens measured? Are they the same as on our side?
07:28 Avery: We measure tokens per model tokenizer; you'll see slight diffs vs your local tokenizer if models differ. Our sheet calls out tokenizer used and includes mapping.
07:36 Liam: Any hidden charges? For Hosted is there any per-request overhead fees or scaling surcharges?
07:41 Avery: No hidden per-request fees for typical use; there are add-ons like extended log retention, private KMS, or dedicated burst capacity which are line items. We'll flag them.
07:53 Dana: What about concurrency limits? For our peak bursts we need high concurrency.
07:58 Samir: Hosted has soft limits; dedicated is for predictable throughput and can be tuned. We support autoscaling policies on dedicated pools and burst capacity add-ons. We'll show target p99 numbers.
08:14 (08:52) Priya: If we do an annual commit, what's the typical discount and exit terms?
08:20 Avery: Annual commitments give the best unit economics; discounts vary by size. We can propose a tiered commit with break clauses and path to Private if needed. Legal will handle specifics.
08:33 Ethan: For private deployment — can we run entirely on-prem with our HSM?
08:38 Samir: Yes, Private on-prem option supports HSM/KMS and air-gapped installs — that is heavier from ops perspective and has separate licensing. It eliminates hosted data plane exposure.
08:49 Dana: Performance differences on prem vs hosted?
08:52 Samir: Varies by hardware. If you bring comparable GPUs, you can match hosted performance. The value is control over data and latency inside your network.
09:02 Liam: For the benchmark we want to test both 1) hosted with route-level caching and 2) dedicated pool with same model and aggressive batching.
09:11 Samir: Good plan. We'll instrument cost per token, p50/p95 latency, and GPU utilization.
09:18 Avery: We'll also show a sensitivity table: token vol vs commit size vs effective unit cost. That helps pick commit level.
09:25 Priya: Can you include amortized costs for infrequently used large context jobs?
09:29 Avery: Yes we'll include examples for sporadic large-context jobs — recommended: keep those on hosted or dedicated with separate route and fallback policies.
09:38 Dana: Any common gotchas?
09:40 Samir: Cache invalidation, tokenization mismatches, and long-tail prompt variance — they all affect realized cost. Also SLOs vs batching — if you over-batch low-latency routes costs go up and user experience degrades.
09:56 (10:12) Ethan: What about GPU types — do you recommend a specific instance for our mix?
10:18 Samir: For mixed medium sequence lengths, the current sweet spot is the latest generation dense GPUs; if you have many long sequences, memory matters — choose higher-memory cards or sharded runtimes. We'll recommend specifics after we see the trace.
10:34 Liam: Any notes on model caching between versions? We worry about rollouts causing warm-up costs.
10:39 Avery: We have rollout strategies with warm caches, can pin versions and can pre-warm KV cache for canaries. There will be a short warm-up spike but our rollout tooling minimizes it.
10:51 Priya: From procurement — what's the PO/contract cadence we should expect?
10:55 Avery: Standard enterprise flow; we'll send contract terms after pricing. Typical pilot -> POC -> commitment -> annual contract. We'll work with your procurement team.
11:06 Dana: Ok let's talk immediate next steps and timeline.
11:09 Priya: We want the pricing sheet this week. If numbers look good we'll schedule the perf run and legal review.
11:15 Avery: We'll get the sheet and security pack to you by Wed 3/18. Samir will run the perf test setup with Ethan for week of 3/23.
11:23 Ethan: I'll provision a VPC and scrub logs and share trace by 3/20.
11:28 Jordan: Dropped links: cost-spreadsheet-template.xlsx, security-pack.pdf, runbook-perf.md (link placeholder).
11:35 Dana: Quick question — do you support per-route quotas and throttles to control spend?
11:40 Samir: Yes route-level quotas, budget caps, and alerting integrate with billing dashboards.
11:46 Priya: Good. Any final risk items we should flag?
11:49 Samir: Main risks: if cache hit rates are lower than modeled, cost outcomes are worse; model choice/quantization may affect accuracy. We'll put sensitivity ranges.
11:59 Avery: Thanks everyone. We'll send the artifacts and follow up.
12:05 Dana: Thanks, talk soon.

Meeting end: ~14:48 PT

References shared: cost-spreadsheet-template.xlsx (link), security-pack.pdf (link), runbook-perf.md (link)
